extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of political theory, historians, and scholars interested in democratic institutions and public opinion
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting and applying criteria about how public opinion operates in democratic systems and how to detect or guard against the 'tyranny of the majority.' Focuses on mechanisms of influence, electoral strategies, institutional safeguards, and social forms of coercion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capture a great standing party
rubrics_metrics.description: To capture one or other of the great standing parties, i.e. to persuade or frighten that party into adopting this view as part of its programme, or making it a plank of the platform.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Most effective course but most difficult; a party is sure to have something to lose as well as to gain by embracing a new dogma. Parties will only take up new questions when they think they will gain thereby. Useful when successful because party candidates will be bound to support it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Form a new party
rubrics_metrics.description: The men who hold the particular view may declare themselves a new party, put forward their own programme, and run their own candidates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Costly and troublesome and may seem ridiculous unless the proposition has already wide support. Even when candidates cannot be carried, a new party serves as an advertisement, alarms the old party, and withdraws voting strength from it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cast organized voting weight to the friendliest party
rubrics_metrics.description: Cast the voting weight of the organized promoters of the doctrine into the scale of whichever party shows the greatest friendliness or seems most open to conversion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A comparatively weak body of opinion may decide results where parties are evenly balanced. The candidates thus carried are not pledged to the group's programme. This tactic can be used as bargaining ('selling out') to secure offices or nominations; it is potent but liable to abuse and can serve as a check on regular parties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use fear of electoral punishment to restrain officials
rubrics_metrics.description: The fear of popular displeasure manifesting at the next election is the most powerful of restraining influences on officials and legislators.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Under balanced authorities it prevents deadlocks and abuse of power; examples include a President emboldened when public opinion sides with him after vetoes, or legislatures hesitating to override vetoes. Frequency of elections brings the prospect of punishment nearer. Exposure and newspaper criticism often check mischief.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize signals that public opinion is effective
rubrics_metrics.description: Public opinion is shown to be influencing politicians when language from moderate men and less partisan newspapers indicates probable sentiment, when organs of the party begin to blame it, or when parties are nearly balanced so small shifts matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are practical indicators that the 'fear' of the polls is being felt: party organs blaming their own party, moderate press language, and small vote fluctuations producing big political impressions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpret electoral fluctuations cautiously
rubrics_metrics.description: The constancy or mutability of electoral bodies is complex: fluctuations may indicate corruptible masses in some districts or an exceptionally thoughtful and unprejudiced element in others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regional variations matter (e.g., more fluctuation in some Western States or in enlightened states like New York and Massachusetts); do not assume a single cause for vote shifts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Employ voluntary and private agencies to promote causes
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the object is to promote a particular cause, form associations and federate them, collect funds, set the press to work, deliver lectures, retain counsel and institute suits, enlist religious magazines and ministers, and send deputations to legislatures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: American expertness in using voluntary agencies gives many ways of making opinion felt. Examples: women's societies, hymn-singing at polling booths, 'Women's Whisky War' where women entered saloons to drive out customers. Such measures also serve to demonstrate strength and recruit sympathy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate the role and limits of party platforms and conventions
rubrics_metrics.description: A 'platform' is usually prepared by a small committee and adopted with little change; its tendency is neither to define nor to convince but to attract and confuse — a mixture of denunciation, declamation, and conciliation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conventions and platforms seldom clarify political opinion; however, in extraordinary times they may record acceptance or rejection of vital propositions (e.g., pre-Civil War, the Silver struggle of 1896). An imprudent platform can expose a party to damaging attacks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for intermittence of American public opinion
rubrics_metrics.description: American political opinion is less continuous and sustained than in Europe because of the pattern of elections (presidential peaks and off-years), leaving long intervals where professional discussion is lacking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many problems (e.g., foreign policy) need uninterrupted and professional study; the intermittent attention in the U.S. can be a structural weakness for complex, long-term issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value independent educated citizens as a check on parties
rubrics_metrics.description: A class of educated, reflective citizens (often prominent in business and professions) who are not blindly attached to parties can set the keynote for city or district opinion and shame or alarm professional politicians.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such independent groups, though numerically small, can be disproportionately powerful in closely balanced systems by throwing votes for candidates they deem capable and honest; their sustained activity and effort to impress masses are what opinion chiefly needs to influence politicians.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and indicators of the 'tyranny of the majority'
rubrics_metrics.description: Tyranny of the majority denotes an abuse by the majority of the powers they enjoy; tyranny consists in the wanton or inequitable use of strength by the stronger — legal in form but oppressive in spirit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Signs include deciding without hearing the minority; suppressing fair and temperate criticism; insisting on restraint where not required by the common interest; forcing contributions to objects citizens disapprove of; subjecting dissenters to social penalties. The essence is wantonness or misuse of authority granted for another purpose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three quarters to examine for majority tyranny
rubrics_metrics.description: To look for signs of majority tyranny examine: (1) the legislation of Congress; (2) the constitutions and statutes of the States; (3) the action of public opinion and sentiment outside the sphere of law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this tripartite checklist to diagnose where and how majority power may be abused; different quarters reveal different modes of possible oppression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess federal constitutional safeguards
rubrics_metrics.description: The Federal Constitution limits the competence of Congress and hedges it with prohibitions; freedoms (speech, religion, debate) are amply secured so some avenues for majority abuse are closed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although powers like taxation and regulation of commerce might theoretically oppress classes, historically such oppressive uses have not prevailed; political actions under excitement (e.g., refusing Abolitionist petitions, some reconstruction measures) are older examples of harsh majority action but are not the typical form of the charge examined.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate state constitutions and statutes for oppression
rubrics_metrics.description: State constitutions now contain many limitations and guarantees so that instances where a minority can legitimately complain are surprisingly few; ordinary statutes rarely repress opinion or personal liberty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some state provisions regulating corporations, railroads, and banks may be unwise and tend to affect the rich, but few statutes are wanton or oppressive. Notable exceptions include California's measures aimed at the Chinese and some Southern statutes enforcing racial separation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize social persecution as a mode of majority tyranny
rubrics_metrics.description: A majority may tyrannize by imposing purely social penalties — from simple disapproval up to insult, injury, and boycotting — outside the sphere of law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such social persecution is the form of tyranny most akin to historical civic enlightenment when absent; in America it is noted as existing only in a few 'dark corners' but remains a relevant criterion to assess civic toleration.
